claim: Body weight is regulated by interoceptive neural circuits that track energy need.
source: Body weight is regulated by interoceptive neural circuits that track energy need, but how the activity of these circuits is altered in obesity remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding of body weight regulation.

claim: High-fat diet attenuates the response of AgRP neurons to food cues.
source: We show that high-fat diet attenuates the response of AgRP neurons to an array of nutritionally-relevant stimuli including food cues, intragastric nutrients, cholecystokinin and ghrelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: High-fat diet attenuates the response of AgRP neurons to intragastric nutrients.
source: We show that high-fat diet attenuates the response of AgRP neurons to an array of nutritionally-relevant stimuli including food cues, intragastric nutrients, cholecystokinin and ghrelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 4.

claim: High-fat diet attenuates the response of AgRP neurons to cholecystokinin.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 5.

claim: High-fat diet attenuates the response of AgRP neurons to ghrelin.

claim: The alterations in AgRP neuron responses are specific to dietary fat but not carbohydrate or protein.
source: These alterations are specific to dietary fat but not carbohydrate or protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential responses to different macronutrients in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Weight loss restores the responsiveness of AgRP neurons to exterosensory cues.
source: Subsequent weight loss restores the responsiveness of AgRP neurons to exterosensory cues but fails to rescue their sensitivity to gastrointestinal hormones or nutrients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing recovery of sensory responses after weight loss.

claim: Weight loss fails to rescue AgRP neuron sensitivity to gastrointestinal hormones.
source: Subsequent weight loss restores the responsiveness of AgRP neurons to exterosensory cues but fails to rescue their sensitivity to gastrointestinal hormones or nutrients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 showing persistent desensitization after weight loss.

claim: Weight loss fails to rescue AgRP neuron sensitivity to nutrients.
source: Subsequent weight loss restores the responsiveness of AgRP neurons to exterosensory cues but fails to rescue their sensitivity to gastrointestinal hormones or nutrients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing persistent desensitization to lipid after weight loss.

claim: Obesity triggers broad dysregulation of hypothalamic hunger neurons.
source: These findings reveal that obesity triggers broad dysregulation of hypothalamic hunger neurons that is incompletely reversed by weight loss and may contribute to the difficulty of maintaining a reduced weight.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The dysregulation of hypothalamic hunger neurons is incompletely reversed by weight loss.
source: These findings reveal that obesity triggers broad dysregulation of hypothalamic hunger neurons that is incompletely reversed by weight loss and may contribute to the difficulty of maintaining a reduced weight.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing persistent alterations after weight loss in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The dysregulation of hypothalamic hunger neurons may contribute to the difficulty of maintaining a reduced weight.
source: These findings reveal that obesity triggers broad dysregulation of hypothalamic hunger neurons that is incompletely reversed by weight loss and may contribute to the difficulty of maintaining a reduced weight.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings regarding their potential clinical significance.

claim: AgRP neurons are located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
source: These neurons are located in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus and are activated by food deprivation (Hahn et al., 1998; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Takahashi and Cone, 2005; van den Top et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: AgRP neurons are activated by food deprivation.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Stimulation of AgRP neurons drives voracious feeding.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Stimulation of AgRP neurons recapitulates the motivational, affective and sensory hallmarks of hunger.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Exogenous leptin fails to reduce food intake in obese animals.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Exposure to HFD for 6 weeks produced reliable weight gain in mice.
source: Exposure to HFD produced reliable weight gain, which was partially reversed after animals were returned to chow (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Weight gain from HFD was partially reversed after animals were returned to chow.
source: Exposure to HFD produced reliable weight gain, which was partially reversed after animals were returned to chow (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Food presentation rapidly inhibited AgRP neurons of lean mice at baseline.
source: As previously reported (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015), food presentation rapidly inhibited AgRP neurons of lean mice at baseline (Figure 1D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and 1G, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: After six weeks on HFD, obese animals showed markedly attenuated responses to presentation of both chow and HFD.
source: After six weeks on HFD, obese animals showed markedly attenuated responses to presentation of both chow and HFD (Figure 1E,F,H,I,J,K,M,N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple panels of Figure 1.

claim: The amount of weight gain in individual mice did not correlate significantly with magnitude of the reduction in AgRP neuron response to food presentation.
source: Of note, the amount of weight gain in individual mice did not correlate significantly with magnitude of the reduction in AgRP neuron response to food presentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that this impairment is not solely due to increased body weight.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The impairment in AgRP neuron response to food presentation is not solely due to increased body weight.
source: Of note, the amount of weight gain in individual mice did not correlate significantly with magnitude of the reduction in AgRP neuron response to food presentation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that this impairment is not solely due to increased body weight.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four weeks of weight loss partially rescued the response of AgRP neurons to chow presentation.
source: Diet-induced obese (DIO) mice were then switched back to chow and tested again after four weeks of weight loss (Figure 1A,B), which partially rescued the response of AgRP neurons to chow (Figure 1E,F,L) but not HFD presentation (Figure 1H,I,O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E, 1F, and 1L.

claim: Four weeks of weight loss did not rescue the response of AgRP neurons to HFD presentation.
source: Diet-induced obese (DIO) mice were then switched back to chow and tested again after four weeks of weight loss (Figure 1A,B), which partially rescued the response of AgRP neurons to chow (Figure 1E,F,L) but not HFD presentation (Figure 1H,I,O).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H, 1I, and 1O.

claim: Control mice maintained on chow exhibited relatively stable neuronal inhibition upon presentation of both foods throughout the time course.
source: In contrast, control mice maintained on chow throughout this time course exhibited relatively stable neuronal inhibition upon presentation of both foods.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Diet-induced obesity reversibly blunts the rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons in response to exterosensory cues.
source: Thus, diet-induced obesity reversibly blunts the rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons in response to exterosensory cues.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings in Figure 1.

claim: The rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons by food presentation is a prediction of impending food consumption.
source: The rapid inhibition of AgRP neurons by food presentation is thought to be a prediction of impending food consumption (Beutler et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: DIO animals consumed significantly fewer calories when presented with chow after an overnight fast compared to lean controls.
source: We found that DIO animals consumed significantly fewer calories when presented with chow after an overnight fast compared to lean controls (Figure 2A and B), as others have observed (Briggs et al., 2011; Ueno et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A and 2B, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: The reduction in caloric intake in DIO animals was not due solely to the lower palatability of chow.
source: This reduction in caloric intake was not due solely to the lower palatability of chow, because DIO mice that were fasted and then allowed to re-feed with HFD also showed a reduction in consumption of HFD when compared either to lean controls (Figure 2C and D) or their own HFD consumption prior to obesity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2C, 2D, and 3E.

claim: DIO mice showed a reduction in consumption of HFD when compared to lean controls.
source: This reduction in caloric intake was not due solely to the lower palatability of chow, because DIO mice that were fasted and then allowed to re-feed with HFD also showed a reduction in consumption of HFD when compared either to lean controls (Figure 2C and D) or their own HFD consumption prior to obesity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: DIO mice showed a reduction in consumption of HFD when compared to their own HFD consumption prior to obesity.
source: This reduction in caloric intake was not due solely to the lower palatability of chow, because DIO mice that were fasted and then allowed to re-feed with HFD also showed a reduction in consumption of HFD when compared either to lean controls (Figure 2C and D) or their own HFD consumption prior to obesity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: The reduction in HFD consumption by DIO animals was not due to sensory-specific satiety or a learned aversion.
source: This reduction in HFD consumption by DIO animals was also not due to sensory-specific satiety or a learned aversion, because when fasted DIO animals were presented with chocolate, a novel palatable food, their food intake remained significantly attenuated (control-chocolate 1.36 kcal vs DIO-chocolate 0.36 kcal, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing chocolate consumption between control and DIO animals.

claim: Fasted DIO animals presented with chocolate consumed significantly less than control animals.
source: This reduction in HFD consumption by DIO animals was also not due to sensory-specific satiety or a learned aversion, because when fasted DIO animals were presented with chocolate, a novel palatable food, their food intake remained significantly attenuated (control-chocolate 1.36 kcal vs DIO-chocolate 0.36 kcal, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing chocolate consumption.

claim: Returning animals to chow for four weeks resulted in moderate weight loss.
source: Animals were returned to chow for four weeks, which resulted in moderate weight loss (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The dietary switch to chow completely restored the consumption of chow and HFD in formerly DIO mice following an overnight fast.
source: However this dietary switch completely restored the consumption of chow and HFD in formerly DIO mice following an overnight fast (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: The behavioral responses to weight gain and loss mirrored the changes in AgRP neuron responses to food.
source: Strikingly, these behavioral responses to weight gain and loss mirrored the changes in AgRP neuron responses to food during this time course (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing behavioral data in Figure 2 with neural data in Figure 1.

claim: HFD exposure inhibits fasting-induced hyperphagia.
source: This reveals that HFD exposure inhibits fasting-induced hyperphagia, which is then rapidly restored following weight loss, and that the anticipatory dynamics of AgRP neurons track these behavioral fluctuations.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Fasting-induced hyperphagia is rapidly restored following weight loss.
source: This reveals that HFD exposure inhibits fasting-induced hyperphagia, which is then rapidly restored following weight loss, and that the anticipatory dynamics of AgRP neurons track these behavioral fluctuations.

claim: The anticipatory dynamics of AgRP neurons track behavioral fluctuations in feeding.
source: This reveals that HFD exposure inhibits fasting-induced hyperphagia, which is then rapidly restored following weight loss, and that the anticipatory dynamics of AgRP neurons track these behavioral fluctuations.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing neural and behavioral data.

claim: DIO animals exhibited attenuated fasting-induced re-feeding when presented with chow or HFD despite limited weight gain over a four-week time course.
source: These DIO animals exhibited attenuated fasting-induced re-feeding when presented with chow or HFD despite limited weight gain over this short time course (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).

claim: Plasma leptin was significantly elevated in DIO animals after four weeks of HFD.
source: As expected, plasma leptin was significantly elevated in DIO animals, but fasting insulin levels were not elevated relative to lean controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Fasting insulin levels were not elevated in DIO animals relative to lean controls after four weeks of HFD.
source: As expected, plasma leptin was significantly elevated in DIO animals, but fasting insulin levels were not elevated relative to lean controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Fasting-induced re-feeding was negatively correlated with leptin levels in DIO animals presented with HFD.
source: Moreover, fasting-induced re-feeding was negatively correlated with leptin levels in DIO animals presented with HFD whereas insulin levels did not significantly correlate with food intake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).

claim: Insulin levels did not significantly correlate with food intake in DIO animals.
source: Moreover, fasting-induced re-feeding was negatively correlated with leptin levels in DIO animals presented with HFD whereas insulin levels did not significantly correlate with food intake (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).

claim: Hyperleptinemia is correlated with decreased fasting-induced hyperphagia in mice early in DIO.

source: As expected, we found that concurrent or pre-stimulation of AgRP neurons caused fed mice to eat more low-fat pellets (Figure 3B, baseline) or HFD (Figure 3C, baseline), and the amount of food consumed was similar between the two protocols (Figure 3B,C, baseline).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Concurrent stimulation of AgRP neurons caused fed mice to eat more low-fat pellets at baseline.
source: As expected, we found that concurrent or pre-stimulation of AgRP neurons caused fed mice to eat more low-fat pellets (Figure 3B, baseline) or HFD (Figure 3C, baseline), and the amount of food consumed was similar between the two protocols (Figure 3B,C, baseline).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pre-stimulation of AgRP neurons caused fed mice to eat more HFD at baseline.

claim: The amount of food consumed was similar between pre-stimulation and concurrent stimulation protocols in fed mice at baseline.

claim: Pre-stimulation did not increase the consumption of low-fat pellets in fasted mice at baseline.
source: In the fasted state, pre-stimulation did not increase the consumption of either diet (Figure 3D,E, baseline), whereas concurrent stimulation caused a small increase in the consumption of low-fat pellets (Figure 3D, baseline) but not HFD (Figure 3E, baseline).

claim: Pre-stimulation did not increase the consumption of HFD in fasted mice at baseline.

claim: Concurrent stimulation caused a small increase in the consumption of low-fat pellets in fasted mice at baseline.

claim: AgRP neurons are already highly active in fasted, lean mice.
source: This result is consistent with the notion that AgRP neurons are already highly active in fasted, lean mice, and therefore that optogenetic stimulation has little additional effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic stimulation results in fasted mice.

claim: Diet-induced obesity greatly reduced the amount of food mice consumed during behavioral tests in the absence of optogenetic stimulation.
source: Consistent with our data from a separate cohort (Figure 2), we found that, in the absence of optogenetic stimulation, diet-induced obesity greatly reduced the amount of food the mice consumed during the behavioral tests.

claim: Diet-induced obesity blunted the hyperphagia in response to presentation of HFD.
source: For example, diet-induced obesity blunted the hyperphagia in response to presentation of HFD (Figure 3C, no stim, baseline versus DIO) as well as the hyperphagia induced by fasting (Figure 3D,E no stim, baseline versus DIO).

claim: Diet-induced obesity blunted the hyperphagia induced by fasting.
source: For example, diet-induced obesity blunted the hyperphagia in response to presentation of HFD (Figure 3C, no stim, baseline versus DIO) as well as the hyperphagia induced by fasting (Figure 3D,E no stim, baseline versus DIO).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons could rescue the decreased feeding in DIO mice.
source: Importantly, we found that optogenetic stimulation of AgRP neurons could rescue this decreased feeding in DIO mice (Figure 3B–E, DIO).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–E.

claim: AgRP neurons are not fully activated by fasting in DIO animals.
source: This suggests AgRP neurons are not fully activated by fasting in DIO animals, and that optogenetic stimulation supplies this missing activation.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation supplies missing activation in DIO animals.
source: This suggests AgRP neurons are not fully activated by fasting in DIO animals, and that optogenetic stimulation supplies this missing activation.

claim: In obese mice, concurrent stimulation induced a bigger effect on food intake than pre-stimulation.

claim: In lean animals the effect of pre-stimulation and concurrent stimulation protocols was indistinguishable in every test performed.

claim: Diet-induced obesity reduces the sensitivity of downstream circuitry to AgRP neuron activity.

evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: Intragastric infusion of lipid, sugar or protein induced progressive, potent, and durable inhibition of AgRP neuron activity in hungry animals at baseline.

claim: AgRP neuron inhibition in response to lipid infusion was significantly decreased in DIO animals compared to their response at baseline.
source: Strikingly, AgRP neuron inhibition in response to lipid infusion was significantly decreased in DIO animals compared to their response at baseline (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–E.

claim: The response of AgRP neurons to glucose was not altered in obese mice.

claim: The response of AgRP neurons to protein was not altered in obese mice.

claim: Obesity induced by HFD selectively desensitizes AgRP neurons to dietary fat.

claim: Ingestion of fat is communicated to AgRP neurons in part through CCK.
source: Ingestion of fat is communicated to AgRP neurons in part through CCK (Beutler et al., 2017) and, consistent with this, we found that obesity also desensitizes AgRP neurons to peripheral CCK (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Obesity desensitizes AgRP neurons to peripheral CCK.
source: Ingestion of fat is communicated to AgRP neurons in part through CCK (Beutler et al., 2017) and, consistent with this, we found that obesity also desensitizes AgRP neurons to peripheral CCK (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–F.

claim: The resistance to dietary fat and CCK persisted after mice had been returned to a low-fat diet and lost weight.
source: Remarkably, this resistance to dietary fat and CCK persisted after mice had been returned to a low-fat diet and lost weight, which normalized their feeding behavior (Figure 2B and D) and neural responses to food cues (Figure 1F and J–L).

claim: Concurrent stimulation causes stronger activation of AgRP circuitry than pre-stimulation.

claim: Greater AgRP neuron activity is required to drive food intake in obese mice.
